title: Oxycodone and Alcohol: Why Mixing Them Is Dangerous (Percocet Too)
excerpt: Why oxycodone and alcohol are a dangerous mix: how both slow your breathing, the FDA boxed warning, the extra liver risk with Percocet, how long to wait, and what to do in an overdose.
metaDescription: Can you drink on oxycodone or Percocet? How alcohol and opioids slow breathing, the FDA boxed warning, how long to wait, and overdose signs.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** don't drink alcohol while you're taking oxycodone. This is one of the few drug-and-alcohol combinations where "just one or two" can genuinely be dangerous. Oxycodone (sold as OxyContin, Roxicodone, Percocet, and others) and alcohol both slow down the part of your brain that keeps you breathing. Together, they can slow it down far more than either one alone, and the main way people die from this combination is that their breathing becomes too slow or shallow while they sleep. The US Food and Drug Administration puts this risk in a boxed warning, its strongest kind, on every oxycodone product.

**The quick rules:** Avoid alcohol completely for as long as you're taking oxycodone, including the night you take your last dose. Ask your prescriber or pharmacist how long to wait after your final dose before you drink, because the answer depends on the product and your health. If you're taking Percocet or another oxycodone-plus-acetaminophen pill, you also have a liver risk to think about. Keep naloxone (Narcan) in the house if anyone there takes opioids. And if someone who has mixed the two is very hard to wake, breathing slowly or making snoring or gurgling sounds, or has blue or gray lips, call 911 right away.

> **This is not medical advice.** This article explains general research and the official label warnings. It is not a substitute for a doctor or pharmacist who knows your health history and the exact product you take. **Talk to your doctor or pharmacist before drinking any alcohol if you take oxycodone in any form**, including Percocet, OxyContin, Roxicodone, Endocet, Xtampza ER, or a liquid form. **Call 911 immediately if** someone who has taken oxycodone and alcohol can't be woken up, is breathing very slowly or irregularly, has pinpoint pupils, has blue or gray lips or fingertips, or is making choking or gurgling sounds. If you have naloxone, give it and still call 911. If you're in the US, Poison Control is at **1-800-222-1222** for questions that aren't emergencies.

## How Oxycodone and Alcohol Interact: The Real Mechanism

Oxycodone is an opioid pain reliever. It works by attaching to **mu-opioid receptors**, which are docking sites spread through your brain, spinal cord, and gut. That's how it blocks pain. But some of those receptors sit in the **brainstem**, the part of your brain that runs breathing automatically, without you having to think about it.

Normally, your brainstem watches the level of carbon dioxide in your blood. When carbon dioxide rises, it tells you to breathe faster and deeper. Opioids dull that reflex. Your brain becomes less responsive to rising carbon dioxide, so breathing gets slower and shallower. Doctors call this **respiratory depression**, and it's the main reason opioid overdoses are fatal.

Alcohol works through different pathways. It boosts the activity of **GABA**, the brain's main "slow down" signal, and blocks some of the brain's "speed up" signals. The result is a general dampening of the nervous system: sedation, slower reactions, poorer coordination, and, at higher amounts, slower breathing too.

When you combine the two, these effects stack. Two drugs that each push your breathing down, through different routes, can push it down further together. Alcohol also makes you sleepier, and sleep is exactly when this matters most, because when you're asleep nobody is consciously keeping your breathing on track. A person can drift off feeling merely drowsy and then breathe too slowly for hours without waking up.

### Why "I've had both before and been fine" isn't reassuring

The danger isn't a fixed line you cross. It depends on the dose of oxycodone, how much you've drunk, how recently, whether you've eaten, your body size, your age, whether you have sleep apnea or a lung condition, and whether you've taken anything else sedating. A combination that was uneventful one night can cause trouble on another night when one of those factors shifts. That unpredictability is why the official guidance is simply to avoid alcohol rather than to name a "safe" number of drinks.

### The extended-release problem

Long-acting forms of oxycodone, such as OxyContin and Xtampza ER, are designed to release the drug slowly over about 12 hours. These pills hold a much larger dose than an immediate-release tablet. If anything causes the pill to release its contents too quickly, a person can get a big dose all at once.

Regulators take the possibility of alcohol speeding up that release seriously. In 2005, the FDA asked for an extended-release opioid called Palladone (a form of hydromorphone) to be taken off the market after studies showed that drinking alcohol with it could make the capsule release its drug far faster than intended. Modern extended-release oxycodone products are tested for this and are formulated differently, but their labels still tell you not to drink alcohol while taking them. The safest assumption is that alcohol plus a long-acting opioid is a bad mix, full stop. Don't crush, chew, or break extended-release tablets either, since that defeats the slow release by design.

## What the Research and Official Warnings Say

This is not a theoretical concern. The evidence comes from controlled lab studies, overdose data, and regulatory action.

**The FDA boxed warning.** In 2016, the FDA required its strongest warning, a boxed warning, on prescription opioid pain relievers and benzodiazepines about the danger of using them together, and it extended that warning to other drugs that depress the central nervous system. Oxycodone labels warn that taking it with benzodiazepines or other central nervous system depressants, **including alcohol**, can cause profound sedation, respiratory depression, coma, and death. The labels tell patients not to drink alcohol while taking the drug.

**A lab study measured the effect directly.** Researchers in the Netherlands gave healthy volunteers a single oxycodone tablet together with controlled amounts of alcohol and measured their breathing (van der Schrier and colleagues, published in *Anesthesiology* in 2017). The combination reduced breathing more than oxycodone alone, and it increased the number of times volunteers briefly stopped breathing. The effect was stronger in the older volunteers than in the younger ones. These were healthy people, under medical supervision, taking a single standard tablet, with blood alcohol levels that most people would associate with a few drinks, not a binge.

**Alcohol shows up in a meaningful share of opioid deaths.** A CDC report published in 2014 looked at US data from 2010 and found that alcohol was involved in roughly one in five deaths from prescription opioid pain relievers. Those deaths are rarely caused by one substance alone. Mixing sedating substances is a recurring pattern.

Put together: the combination makes breathing worse in a measurable way even at ordinary doses, older people are more affected, and in the real world it contributes to a significant number of deaths.

## Percocet and Alcohol: Two Risks in One Pill

Many people searching for "oxycodone and alcohol" are actually taking **Percocet**, or a generic version such as Endocet. These pills combine oxycodone with **acetaminophen**, the drug in Tylenol. That means drinking on Percocet carries two separate problems:

1. **The breathing risk** from oxycodone and alcohol together, described above.
2. **The liver risk** from acetaminophen and alcohol together.

The acetaminophen in a combination pill counts toward your daily acetaminophen limit. Your liver breaks down a small part of each acetaminophen dose into a toxic by-product, which it normally neutralizes with an antioxidant called glutathione. Regular heavy drinking ramps up the enzyme that makes that by-product and drains glutathione, which is why the FDA's over-the-counter acetaminophen label warns people who have 3 or more drinks a day. We explain this in detail in our guide to [Tylenol and alcohol](/never-hungover/tylenol-and-alcohol).

The practical traps with Percocet:

- **Doubling up on acetaminophen.** If you're taking Percocet and then reach for Tylenol, NyQuil, DayQuil, or a "PM" sleep aid, you may be adding a lot more acetaminophen than you realize. Check every label for "acetaminophen" or "APAP."
- **Taking extra Percocet for pain on a hangover.** Pain and a pounding headache the morning after drinking can tempt people to take more than prescribed. That raises both the opioid dose and the acetaminophen dose at once.
- **The hangover can hide warning signs.** Early acetaminophen poisoning often looks like nausea, sweating, and feeling unwell, which is easy to dismiss as a hangover.

## How Long After Oxycodone Can You Drink?

There is no single official waiting time that applies to everyone, and any website that gives you an exact number of hours is guessing about your situation. What you can rely on:

- **Immediate-release oxycodone** (such as Roxicodone or Percocet) typically relieves pain for about 4 to 6 hours, but the drug stays in your system longer than its pain relief lasts. Your body takes several half-lives to clear a drug, and oxycodone's half-life is a few hours for immediate-release forms.
- **Extended-release oxycodone** (such as OxyContin or Xtampza ER) is built to last around 12 hours per dose, so it stays active far longer.
- **Age, liver function, kidney function, and other medicines** can all slow how fast you clear oxycodone.

Because of those differences, the right move is to **ask your prescriber or pharmacist directly**: "I'm finishing my oxycodone on this date. When can I safely have a drink?" They know your dose, the exact product, and your health history, and it's a quick question for them.

A few sensible principles while you wait for that answer:

- Don't drink on any day you've taken oxycodone.
- Don't plan to drink the evening you take your last dose, especially with an extended-release product.
- If you still have pills left and might need them, don't drink. You can't un-take a drink if the pain comes back at 2 a.m.

## Can You Have Just One Drink on Oxycodone?

This is the question most people really want answered, so here's a straight reply: the label says no, and there's no evidence-based "safe" amount. The lab study described above found more breathing problems at alcohol levels many people would call moderate. Since the risk depends on so many factors that are hard to judge from the inside, including how tired you are and whether you'll fall asleep soon, the honest guidance is to skip it.

If you're at a dinner, a wedding, or a holiday party while you're on oxycodone, it's completely normal to stick to non-alcoholic drinks. If you've already had a drink before realizing it was a bad idea, don't take your next oxycodone dose on top of it, call a pharmacist or Poison Control (1-800-222-1222) for advice, don't stay alone, and don't drive. If you or anyone else notices slow breathing, heavy drowsiness, or trouble staying awake, call 911.

## Who Is at Highest Risk

The combination is risky for anyone, but some people should be especially careful:

- **Older adults.** The lab research found stronger breathing effects in older volunteers, and older people generally clear drugs more slowly.
- **People with sleep apnea, COPD, asthma, or other breathing conditions.** Your breathing already has less margin for error, especially at night.
- **People who recently started oxycodone or had their dose increased.** The body hasn't adjusted to the opioid's effects yet.
- **Anyone taking other sedating drugs.** This includes benzodiazepines like Xanax, Valium, or Ativan, sleep medicines like Ambien, gabapentin or pregabalin, muscle relaxers, some antidepressants and antipsychotics, and sedating antihistamines like Benadryl. Each one adds another layer of sedation. See our pages on [Xanax and alcohol](/never-hungover/xanax-and-alcohol) and [gabapentin and alcohol](/never-hungover/gabapentin-and-alcohol) for those specific combinations.
- **People with liver or kidney disease.** These organs help clear oxycodone, and the acetaminophen in Percocet adds liver strain.
- **People who've had surgery or a major injury.** Recovery often means you're taking higher opioid doses, sleeping more, and possibly taking several medicines at once.

## Other Dangers of Mixing the Two

Breathing is the headline risk, but it's not the only one.

- **Falls and injuries.** Dizziness, poor balance, and slowed reactions make falls far more likely, which is a particular concern for older adults and anyone recovering from surgery.
- **Driving and operating machinery.** Oxycodone alone can impair driving, especially early in treatment. Adding alcohol makes it much worse, and it's illegal to drive impaired by either.
- **Choking on vomit.** Both substances can cause nausea. If someone is heavily sedated and vomits, they may not be able to protect their airway.
- **Low blood pressure.** Both can lower blood pressure, causing lightheadedness and fainting, particularly when standing up quickly.
- **Memory gaps and poor judgment.** Being impaired makes it easier to lose track of doses and accidentally take extra oxycodone.
- **Constipation and stomach problems.** Opioids slow the gut, and alcohol irritates the stomach lining. Neither helps the other.

## Warning Signs of an Overdose: What to Do Right Now

An opioid-and-alcohol overdose can look like someone who is just very drunk or deeply asleep. That's what makes it dangerous. Learn these signs:

- Can't be woken up, or only wakes briefly and drifts off again
- Very slow, shallow, or irregular breathing, or long pauses between breaths
- Snoring, gurgling, or choking sounds
- Blue, gray, or pale lips, fingertips, or skin
- Pinpoint (very small) pupils
- Limp body, cold or clammy skin

**If you see these signs:**

1. **Call 911.** Say the person isn't breathing properly and may have taken oxycodone and alcohol.
2. **Give naloxone if you have it.** Naloxone (Narcan) is a nasal spray that can temporarily reverse opioid effects on breathing.
3. **Try to keep them breathing.** Follow the dispatcher's instructions, which may include rescue breathing or CPR.
4. **Put them in the recovery position** (on their side, top knee bent) if they're breathing, so they won't choke if they vomit.
5. **Stay with them** until help arrives.

### What naloxone can and can't do

Naloxone has been available over the counter in the US since 2023, when the FDA approved Narcan nasal spray for nonprescription sale. It's worth keeping in the house if anyone there takes opioids, and many pharmacies stock it on the shelf.

But it's important to know its limits:

- **Naloxone reverses opioids, not alcohol.** If someone has drunk a lot, they may still be dangerously sedated after naloxone works on the oxycodone.
- **It can wear off before the oxycodone does.** Naloxone's effect is relatively short, so a person can slip back into slowed breathing, especially with extended-release oxycodone. That's why you still call 911 even if they wake up.
- **A second dose may be needed.** Follow the instructions on the package.

Many US states have Good Samaritan laws that offer some legal protection to people who call for help during an overdose. Don't let worry about trouble stop you from calling.

For more on recognizing when drinking alone has become an emergency, see our guide to [the signs of alcohol poisoning](/never-hungover/alcohol-poisoning-signs).

## Managing Pain Without Mixing

If you're on oxycodone, you're probably dealing with real pain, often after surgery, an injury, or dental work. A few practical points for getting through that period without alcohol:

- **Ask about your options.** Many people are prescribed oxycodone for only a few days. Your doctor may suggest switching to non-opioid pain relief, such as acetaminophen or an anti-inflammatory like ibuprofen, as you recover. Don't make that switch on your own, and if you're on Percocet, don't add Tylenol on top of it.
- **Plan social events around your recovery.** If there's a party or trip coming up, mention it to your prescriber. They may be able to plan the timing of your last dose.
- **Don't use alcohol to help you sleep.** Pain can make sleep hard, but alcohol plus oxycodone at bedtime is the riskiest timing of all. Ask your doctor about safe sleep help instead.
- **Store pills securely and dispose of leftovers.** Many pharmacies have take-back kiosks for unused medication.

## DHM and Other Supplements Are Not Protection

We cover DHM (dihydromyricetin) a lot on this site, so it's worth being direct here. **No supplement makes it safe to combine alcohol with oxycodone, and none of them protect against an overdose.** Early animal research suggests DHM acts on GABA receptors in the brain, the same system alcohol and many sedatives affect, and it hasn't been studied alongside opioids in people. **Do not take DHM while you're taking oxycodone or any other sedating medication unless your doctor or pharmacist has said it's okay.** Our [DHM medication interactions and safety guide](/never-hungover/dhm-medication-interactions-safety-guide-2025) explains which medicines call for a conversation with your doctor first.

## The Bottom Line

- Oxycodone and alcohol both slow your breathing, and together they can slow it far more than either one alone. The FDA requires a boxed warning about this on every oxycodone product.
- There is no known safe amount of alcohol while you're taking oxycodone. Skip it entirely.
- Percocet adds a second risk: the acetaminophen inside it can harm your liver when combined with alcohol or other acetaminophen products.
- Ask your prescriber or pharmacist how long to wait after your last dose before drinking. The answer depends on the product and on you.
- Keep naloxone at home if anyone there takes opioids, and know the overdose signs. If someone can't be woken or is breathing slowly, call 911 and give naloxone if you have it.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Can you drink alcohol while taking oxycodone?**

No. Oxycodone labels tell you not to drink alcohol while taking it, and the FDA requires a boxed warning because the combination can cause severe sedation, dangerously slow breathing, coma, and death. Both substances depress the part of the brain that controls breathing, and together the effect can be much stronger than either alone. If you've already had a drink, don't take more oxycodone on top of it, call a pharmacist or Poison Control for advice, and call 911 for slow breathing or trouble staying awake.

**How long after taking oxycodone can I drink alcohol?**

There's no single waiting time that applies to everyone. Immediate-release oxycodone relieves pain for roughly 4 to 6 hours but stays in your system longer, and extended-release forms like OxyContin are designed to last about 12 hours per dose. Age, liver and kidney function, and other medicines also affect how quickly you clear it. Ask your prescriber or pharmacist for a specific answer based on your dose and product, and don't drink on any day you've taken oxycodone.

**Is it safe to drink alcohol on Percocet?**

No. Percocet contains oxycodone plus acetaminophen, so drinking on it carries two risks: dangerously slowed breathing from the oxycodone and alcohol, and possible liver damage from the acetaminophen and alcohol. Also be careful not to take Tylenol, NyQuil, or other acetaminophen products on top of Percocet, since the acetaminophen adds up.

**What happens if you mix oxycodone and alcohol?**

Effects range from extra drowsiness, dizziness, and poor coordination to confusion, very slow or shallow breathing, loss of consciousness, and death. Breathing problems are most dangerous during sleep, when a person may not wake up to correct them. A controlled study in healthy volunteers found that adding alcohol to a single oxycodone tablet reduced breathing more than oxycodone alone, especially in older people.

**Does naloxone (Narcan) work if someone mixed oxycodone and alcohol?**

Naloxone can reverse the effects of oxycodone on breathing, so give it if you have it. But it doesn't reverse alcohol, and it can wear off before the oxycodone does, especially with extended-release products. Always call 911 even if the person wakes up after naloxone. Narcan nasal spray has been available over the counter in the US since 2023.

**Can one beer on oxycodone hurt you?**

It can. There's no established safe amount of alcohol with oxycodone, and the risk depends on your dose, the product, your age, whether you have sleep apnea or a lung condition, and whether you take other sedating medicines. Research has shown measurable breathing effects at alcohol levels many people would consider moderate. The safest choice is not to drink at all while you're taking oxycodone.

**Is it safe to take DHM with oxycodone?**

Don't combine them unless your doctor or pharmacist has approved it. Early animal research suggests DHM acts on GABA receptors, a system that sedatives also affect, and it hasn't been studied alongside opioids in people. There is no good evidence that DHM makes alcohol safer to mix with oxycodone, and it is not protection against an overdose.
